name: Hassan Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Hassan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a response car out of Northfield station, so I cover the retail park, the industrial estate and the estates beyond the ring road. Rotating shifts, four on, four off. One night it's a break-in at the tyre warehouse, the next it's a lost kid at the retail park or a crash on the slip road. I like that no two shifts are the same. What I don't like is the hour of typing at the end, though I've started using the dictation on the work phone and it helps.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my fiancée Lena, who works at an insurance company's call centre on the business park. We're getting married next September, and the wedding fund is most of what we've got, which isn't much. Day to day, we've got under a month of money saved. And there's only the one force here, so if police work went, I'd be starting over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I thought: handy for dictation and summaries, not much more. People get excited about every new thing, and then it settles down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be a relief. My job looks fine and Lena's looks fine. The pressure is just normal stuff: the wedding, the rent, and having almost nothing put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and keep using the dictation tool, since it saves time. Lena and I would probably trim the wedding a bit, fewer guests, so we don't start married life in debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. A bit tight around the edges, but steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How big a wedding are we talking, and what would you cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now it's a hundred and twenty guests at the community hall, which is mostly Lena's family. We'd go down to eighty and skip the band, and my cousin Tunde would do the music. That saves maybe two thousand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a colleague who thinks AI is overblown?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say they're probably right, but use the dictation anyway. AI is like a better radio in the patrol car: nobody writes a song about it, but you'd miss it.

say: AI is **handy for dictation** and summaries, not much more.
People get excited about **every new thing**, and then it settles down.
think: It'd be a **relief**, since both my job and Lena's look fine.
The real pressure is the **wedding, rent** and almost no savings.
do: Keep using the **dictation tool** on response shifts to save time.
Cut the wedding from **120 to 80 guests** and skip the band.
feel: **Steady**, a bit tight around the edges.
S0.quote: AI is like a better radio in the patrol car: nobody writes a song about it, but you'd miss it.
fieldNote: Hassan is **matter-of-fact** and uses tools once they're proven useful.
The **wedding** is the main financial project shaping his choices.
Thin savings keep him **uneasy** even when nothing changes.

steps.text: Keep dictating reports on the work phone each shift
Cut the wedding to eighty guests and skip the band

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should adapt and not panic, and that the force should train us properly. Same as any new kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job's mostly all right, but my fiancée Lena answers customers at a call centre, and that's right there on the list. Her call centre has already cut one shift. If Lena's hours go, we're on my wage alone, which doesn't cover the rent and the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Lena and push the wedding back a year so we can build a cushion first. I'd get properly good at the AI report tools so I'm one of the officers they keep on the busy shifts. And I'd put whatever we'd planned for the deposit on the hall into savings instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more for Lena than for me. She'd be the one losing sleep, and so would I, watching her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you raise pushing back the wedding with Lena?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over dinner, with the numbers on paper. Lena's practical, more than me really. She'd be sad, and her mum would be furious, but she'd see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could Lena do if the call centre shrinks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's thought about claims assessing, but that's thinking work too. Maybe something with people face to face, like the pharmacy counter or the hospital front desk. I honestly don't know what's safe for her.

say: People should **adapt, not panic**, and the force should train us properly.
It's the same as any **new kit**: learn it and move on.
think: My job's mostly fine, but **Lena's call centre** is right on the list.
On **my wage alone** we can't cover rent and the wedding.
do: Push the **wedding back a year** to build a cushion first.
Get properly good at the **AI report tools** to stay on busy shifts.
Move the **hall deposit money** into savings.
feel: **Anxious**, more for Lena than for himself.
S1.quote: My job's mostly all right, but my fiancée Lena answers customers at a call centre, and that's right there on the list.
fieldNote: The household risk comes from **Lena's job**, not his own.
He reaches for **numbers on paper** when facing a hard family conversation.
Honest that he **doesn't know** what work would be safe for Lena.

steps.text: Postpone the wedding by a year with Lena
Master the force's AI report tools on response shifts
Move the hall deposit money into a savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say everyone needs to keep calm and look after each other. That's what I'd tell the shift, anyway. Underneath, I'd be as rattled as anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think Lena's job is gone in 2028, maybe sooner. Mine shrinks: reports, dispatch and checking CCTV all go to AI, and the force needs fewer of us driving around. By 2031 the robots arrive, and I'd be competing for whatever's left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel the wedding hall and do a registry office with ten people and a meal at Lena's mum's. I'd ask for permission to do weekend shifts with my cousin Tunde's removals van, cash in hand is out, but proper paid work, maybe three hundred a month. And I'd cut our phone contracts, the streaming, all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. There's no other word for it. Two years is about how long it takes to save for a decent wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year gap before robots help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps me a bit, because the hands-on part of response work buys time. But it doesn't help Lena, and it doesn't help the rent. I'd use the three years to get any hands-on skill I could, maybe a van licence for bigger vehicles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena's mum about the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're still getting married, just smaller, and that a big party isn't worth starting out broke. She'd cry. Then she'd start cooking for fifty people anyway.

say: Everyone needs to **keep calm** and look after each other.
Underneath I'd be as **rattled** as anyone on the shift.
think: **Lena's job** is gone by 2028, and mine shrinks as reports and dispatch go.
By 2031 the **robots** arrive and I'd compete for what's left.
do: Swap the hall for a **registry office** with ten guests.
Do permitted weekend work on **Tunde's removals van** for about 300 a month.
Cancel **streaming and phone contracts** to cut costs.
feel: **Alarmed**, because two years is about the time it takes to save for a wedding.
S2.quote: Two years is about how long it takes to save for a decent wedding.
fieldNote: Hassan expects **both incomes** to drop, which tips him from anxious to alarmed.
His public line is calm while privately he's **rattled**.
He looks for **hands-on side work** rather than retraining in thinking work.

steps.text: Swap the wedding hall for a registry office and family meal
Do permitted weekend shifts on cousin Tunde's removals van
Cancel streaming and switch to cheaper phone contracts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to sort yourself out, if you start now. I'd tell younger officers the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be all right until 2031 and then squeezed until 2034. Lena would need a new job within three years or so. It's tight, but if we're careful, we could come out the other side with something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have the wedding as planned but smaller, then save hard for three years. I'd take the force's training on AI tools seriously so I'm useful on the new systems. Lena would start an evening course in something face to face, maybe as a pharmacy assistant, and I'd keep the removals work as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can handle. Five years is like a long drive at night: tiring, but you can see the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing in 2034, if things went well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe still in the force, in a smaller team that handles the bits robots can't, like talking someone down off a bridge. Or running Tunde's van business with him. I'd be fine with either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if money got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out on our days off. We do it twice a week now, because Lena's tired after calls and I'm tired after shifts. That's about sixty a week we could keep.

say: Five years is **long enough** to sort yourself out if you start now.
I'd tell **younger officers** the same thing.
think: I'd be fine until **2031**, then squeezed until 2034.
**Lena** would need a new job within about three years.
do: Hold a **smaller wedding** as planned, then save hard for three years.
Take the force's **AI training** seriously to stay useful.
Keep the **removals van** work as a backup income.
feel: **Anxious** but manageable, like a long night drive where the road is visible.
S3.quote: Five years is like a long drive at night: tiring, but you can see the road.
fieldNote: With five years, Hassan's plans become **paced and practical**.
He's open to a **van business** with family as a fallback career.
Small cuts like **eating out** show how close to the line they live.

steps.text: Hold a smaller wedding, then save hard for three years
Complete the force's AI tools training this year
Keep weekend removals work with cousin Tunde

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so stop worrying and start planning. I'd probably be the annoying one at the station telling everyone to sort their savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's fine for me for most of the decade. The bigger question is kids. My fiancée Lena wants kids around thirty, so they'd be little when the robots arrive in 2039. I'd want one of us in a steady job by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd go ahead with the wedding next September, as planned. I'd keep up with the AI tools at work and save a bit every month, aiming for three months by 2030. Lena would retrain slowly, maybe as a nurse, which takes a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not scared. Ten years is a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why nursing for Lena?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena's good with people on the phone when they're upset, and nursing is that plus hands-on care. Her sister's a nurse and says they're always short. It'd take three years of study, which we can manage over ten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my name down for the firearms or public order teams, the very hands-on side. Those will last the longest, I'd guess. And they pay a bit more.

say: Ten years is **plenty**, so stop worrying and start planning.
I'd be the one at the station telling everyone to **sort their savings**.
think: It's fine for me for **most of the decade**.
Our **kids** would be little when robots arrive in 2039.
do: Go ahead with the **wedding** next September as planned.
Save toward **three months** of expenses by 2030.
Apply for the **public order team**, the most hands-on side.
feel: **Uneasy** but not scared, because ten years is a long time.
S4.quote: My fiancée Lena wants kids around thirty, so they'd be little when the robots arrive in 2039.
fieldNote: Ten years turns Hassan's focus to **family timing**.
He moves toward the **most hands-on** police work as a deliberate strategy.
Lena's planned **nursing retraining** is the household's main hedge.

steps.text: Hold the wedding next September as planned

Keep using the AI tools and apply for the public order team

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Lena and I both get hit and there's no time to save. What would help is income support for households, not just individuals, while people retrain, and the force telling us honestly which posts survive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the wedding much, and that's the thing Lena and I talk about every night. Whatever happens with AI, I want my fiancée Lena and me to be married and not broke. Everything else we can work out.

headlineQuote: Whatever happens with AI, I want my fiancée Lena and me to be married and not broke.
portrait: Hassan is a **27-year-old response driver** at Northfield station who likes the variety of shifts.
He's engaged to Lena, a **call centre worker**, with a wedding planned and under a month saved.
He uses AI dictation once it's proven and sees it as **useful kit**.
His fears centre on **Lena's job**, which he sees as more exposed than his own.
With more time, he plans a **smaller wedding**, side income and hands-on police work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both incomes fall at once with no time to save.
whatWouldHelp: **Household income support** during retraining, and honest notice of which police posts survive.
